title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Conclusion & Perspectives
text:
This project investigated whether the nominal 10Y US Treasury yield constitutes a reliable indicator of gold prices, using daily data from June 2011 to June 2026. The question was deliberately framed around the nominal yield — rather than the theoretically superior real yield — to assess the practical signal value of the most immediately observable rate.
The empirical evidence is clear: the nominal yield does not structurally explain gold prices. Cointegration tests fail on both the full period and the pre-2022 sub-period, and rolling OLS estimates confirm that explanatory power is episodic at best — activating in specific low-inflation macro regimes (notably 2014–2016 and 2018–2022) and collapsing elsewhere. The Z-score analysis further reveals that gold has been operating in historically anomalous territory since 2024, driven by factors that lie outside the scope of this analysis and that the nominal yield alone cannot capture.
This result is not a failure — it is informative. The nominal yield conflates the real rate and breakeven inflation, two forces with opposing effects on gold. Its inability to track gold consistently is precisely what the Fisher decomposition predicts:
\[\text{Nominal Yield} = \text{Real Yield} + \text{Breakeven Inflation Rate}\]
A natural extension of this work would be to decompose the nominal yield using TIPS and breakeven data (available via FRED), and test whether the real yield component restores the structural relationship documented in the academic literature.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Conclusion & Perspectives
text:
Perspectives — A Daily Monitoring Proposition
Disclaimer: this project is a personal and non-professional one, conducted for practice purposes. The monitoring proposition below is a technical demonstration of what a production pipeline could look like, not an investment tool.

Rationale
While the nominal yield fails as a structural predictor of gold, this limitation is itself analytically useful. The moments when the relationship anomalously activates — or dramatically breaks down — are precisely the moments worth monitoring. A sustained Z-score above +2σ does not signal mean-reversion; it signals that gold is decoupling from its rate environment, which is a macro observation of independent interest to any multi-asset allocator.
The proposed monitor answers one question each morning:

Is gold currently behaving as a rate-sensitive asset, or has it decoupled?



Target audience
A macro analyst or multi-asset allocator who holds gold as a portfolio component and wants a daily, low-noise signal on the current regime — not a trading signal, but a regime awareness indicator.


Production architecture
The pipeline is designed to be lightweight and cost-free, running entirely on Azure free-tier services:
Azure Function (timer trigger — daily, 8:00 AM CET)
        ↓
R script — 3 Alpha Vantage API calls → append to Parquet → Azure Blob Storage
        ↓
R script — recompute rolling metrics (β, R², Z-score) on updated panel
        ↓
Generate static HTML dashboard (plotly / htmlwidgets)
        ↓
Azure Static Web Apps (free tier)
        ├── /index.html          ← daily monitor dashboard
        └── /notebooks/          ← Quarto analytical notebooks

Limitations
This monitor uses the nominal yield only. It does not incorporate real yield data, breakeven inflation, the DXY, or any other explanatory variable. It should be interpreted exclusively as a regime diagnostic — a signal that something unusual is happening in the gold/yield relationship, not an explanation of why, and certainly not a prediction of what comes next.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Cointegration Testing (Sub-period 2011–2021)
text:
The full-period Johansen test (2011–2026) failed to confirm cointegration between gold and the 10Y nominal treasury yield. However, visual inspection of the raw series suggests a structural break around 2022, when gold and yields began moving simultaneously — a pattern inconsistent with the classical inverse relationship.
This is corroborated by J.P. Morgan Private Bank (2026)1, which documents a post-2022 asymmetric regime where gold resists yield increases while still responding to yield decreases.
We therefore re-run the Johansen test on the 2011–2021 sub-period, isolating the classical regime before the structural break.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Cointegration Testing (Sub-period 2011–2021)
text:
Conclusion
The Johansen test fails to confirm cointegration even on the pre-2022 sub-period. Both the Trace statistic (12.50) and the Maximum Eigenvalue statistic (10.94) fall below their respective 5% critical values (19.96 and 15.67), and even below the 10% thresholds.
This result is analytically meaningful, and consistent with the theoretical limitation identified in the introduction: the nominal yield embeds both the real rate and inflation expectations (breakeven inflation rate), two forces with opposing effects on gold. Even before 2022, this conflation is likely sufficient to prevent a stable cointegrating vector from emerging.
A static long-run equilibrium framework is therefore inappropriate when working with the nominal yield as a proxy for gold’s opportunity cost. We consequently abandon the VECM specification and pivot to a rolling OLS approach, which is better suited to capturing a relationship whose strength and direction evolve over time — and whose instability is itself the central finding of this analysis.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Stationarity Testing
text:
Before testing for any long-run relationship between gold and nominal treasury yields, we need to establish the order of integration of each series.
A series is said to be stationary (I(0)) if it fluctuates around a constant mean with constant variance over time. A series is integrated of order 1 (I(1)) if it is non-stationary in level but becomes stationary after taking first differences.
Cointegration — and the VECM that follows — requires both series to be I(1). If one series is I(0) and the other I(1), the framework collapses.
The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test is a standard tool for this. It tests the null hypothesis of a unit root (non-stationarity) against the alternative of stationarity.
\[H_0: \text{series has a unit root (non-stationary)}\] \[H_1: \text{series is stationary}\]
A p-value below 0.05 leads us to reject \(H_0\) and conclude stationarity.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Introduction
text:
Gold is one of the most studied assets in macroeconomic finance. Unlike equities or bonds, it generates no cash flow — no dividend, no coupon. Its value is therefore largely driven by opportunity cost: what an investor gives up by holding gold instead of a yield-bearing asset.
The academic literature consistently points to the real 10Y Treasury yield (nominal yield minus inflation expectations) as the canonical driver of this opportunity cost. When real yields rise, the relative attractiveness of gold falls, and vice versa. This theoretical relationship is well established:

Jermann (2023, NBER): a no-arbitrage pricing model calibrated on 10Y real US Treasury rates successfully replicates gold price fluctuations since 2007.
Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (2021): a 1 percentage point rise in the long-term real rate is associated with a 13.1% decline in the real gold price over the period 1971–2021.
J.P. Morgan Private Bank (2026): documents a structural break post-2022, where even the real yield relationship weakened — gold became asymmetrically reactive, rising when yields fall but resisting when yields rise.

However, the real yield requires inflation expectations data — typically derived from TIPS spreads — which introduces additional complexity and data dependencies. The nominal 10Y Treasury yield, by contrast, is universally available, instantly observable, and widely monitored by market participants.
This raises a practical and empirically interesting question:

Is the nominal 10Y Treasury yield a good indicator of gold prices?

This is distinct from the theoretical question of whether real yields drive gold. It asks whether the nominal yield — which embeds both the real rate and inflation expectations (i.e breakeven inflation rate)— retains enough signal to track gold in practice. If it does, it simplifies the analytical framework considerably. If it does not, understanding why it fails is itself informative.
This project investigates this question empirically using daily data from June 2011 to June 2026, sourced from the Alpha Vantage API.
Disclaimer : This project is a personal and non-professional one, conducted for practice purposes.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Introduction
text:
Hypotheses

H1 — Long-run equilibrium relationship
The nominal 10Y US Treasury yield is a significant negative predictor of the gold price, and a stable long-run cointegrating relationship exists between the two series.
Formally, if both series are integrated of order 1 — i.e. I(1) — we expect to find at least one cointegrating vector such that:
\[\text{Gold}_t = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{NominalYield}_t + \varepsilon_t\]
where \(\varepsilon_t\) is stationary, and \(\beta < 0\).


H2 — Mean-reverting residual
The residual \(\varepsilon_t\) from the long-run relationship is mean-reverting. Deviations from equilibrium are temporary and self-correcting.
This implies that when gold is overpriced relative to what the nominal yield level implies, it will tend to revert downward — and vice versa. The normalized residual therefore constitutes an analytical signal:
\[z_t = \frac{\varepsilon_t - \mu_\varepsilon}{\sigma_\varepsilon}\]
\[z_t > +2 \Rightarrow \text{gold expensive relative to nominal yields}\] \[z_t < -2 \Rightarrow \text{gold cheap relative to nominal yields}\]

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Introduction
section: Why the Nominal Yield May Fall Short
text:
Why the Nominal Yield May Fall Short
The nominal yield is the sum of two components:
\[\text{Nominal Yield} = \text{Real Yield} + \text{Breakeven inflation rate}\]
Both components have opposing effects on gold: - Real yield ↑ → gold less attractive (opportunity cost rises) → gold ↓ - Inflation expectations ↑ → gold more attractive (inflation hedge) → gold ↑
When inflation is rising, both the nominal yield and gold can increase simultaneously — creating a positive correlation that masks or reverses the theoretical negative relationship. This is precisely the dynamic observed post-2022, and it is a structural limitation of using the nominal yield as a proxy.
Understanding this mechanism will allow us to interpret our empirical results in context.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Introduction
text:
Analytical Framework
The analysis proceeds in four steps:

Stationarity testing — Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests on each series in level and first difference, to confirm both are I(1).
Cointegration testing — Johansen test on the full period (2011–2026) and the pre-break sub-period (2011–2021), to determine whether a stable long-run equilibrium exists.
Rolling OLS — Estimation of \(\beta\) on rolling windows of 60, 252, and 504 days to assess the time-varying nature of the relationship and its robustness across window sizes.
Regime diagnostic — Z-score analysis of rolling residuals to identify periods where gold is operating within vs. beyond its historically normal range relative to nominal yields.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Cointegration Testing
text:
Two I(1) series are said to be cointegrated if a linear combination of them is stationary. Intuitively, even though each series wanders randomly on its own, they move together in the long run — they share a common stochastic trend.
In our case, cointegration between gold and the 10Y yield would mean that deviations from the long-run equilibrium relationship are temporary and self-correcting — which is precisely what H1 and H2 require.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Cointegration Testing
text:
The Johansen Test
The Johansen test is the standard multivariate framework for cointegration. It tests for the number of cointegrating vectors \(r\) in a system of I(1) series.
We test sequentially:
\[H_0: r = 0 \quad \text{(no cointegration)}\] \[H_0: r \leq 1 \quad \text{(at most one cointegrating vector)}\]
Rejecting \(r = 0\) and failing to reject \(r \leq 1\) confirms exactly one cointegrating relationship — which is what we expect in a bivariate system.
The test comes in two variants:

Trace test : tests whether the number of cointegrating vectors is less than \(r\)
Maximum eigenvalue test : tests whether there are exactly \(r\) cointegrating vectors

We report both.

For each test, we compare the test statistic to the critical value at 5%:

For the Trace test, for \(H_0: r = 0\) , the test-statistic is of 17.39, which is below the critical value at 5% (19.96) and even below the critical value at 10% (17.85).
For the Eigenvalue test, also for \(H_0: r = 0\) , the test-statistic is of 13.24, which is also below the critical values at 5% (15.67) and at 10% (13.75).

We expected this first H0 to be rejected, but in both cases we fail to reject it.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Cointegration Testing
text:
Conclusion
The cointegration test has failed on the full time window. Still, by looking at the descriptive statistics, we see graphical evidences of a potential inflexion point around 2022 in the relationship of the two curves. We will therefore re-investigate the cointegration between 2011 and 2022.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Rolling OLS
text:
The cointegration tests on both the full period (2011–2026) and the pre-break sub-period (2011–2021) failed to confirm a stable long-run equilibrium between gold and the nominal 10Y Treasury yield.
Rather than concluding prematurely that no relationship exists, we investigate whether the nominal yield retains any episodic explanatory power over gold. The rolling OLS approach estimates \(\beta\) on a moving window, allowing us to observe how — and when — the sensitivity of gold to the nominal yield activates or disappears over time.
We estimate the following regression on each rolling window \([t-w, t]\):
\[\text{Gold}_t = \alpha_t + \beta_t \cdot \text{NominalYield}_t + \varepsilon_t\]
where \(w\) is the window size. We compare three window sizes as a robustness check:

60 days (~3 months) — reactive, but noisy
252 days (~1 year) — standard
504 days (~2 years) — smooth, but slow to detect breaks

If conclusions hold across all three windows, the result is robust to this arbitrary choice.

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Rolling OLS
text:
Setup


Code
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)

panel <- read_parquet("../data/macro_panel.parquet")

# Generic rolling OLS function
roll_ols <- function(data, window) {
  n <- nrow(data)
  map_dfr((window + 1):n, function(i) {
    fit <- lm(gold ~ yield, data = data[(i - window):i, ])
    tibble(
      date  = data$date[i],
      beta  = coef(fit)[2],
      r2    = summary(fit)$r.squared,
      resid = tail(residuals(fit), 1)
    )
  })
}

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Rolling OLS
text:
Residual Z-score — H2 Signal (252-day window)


Code
results_all <- results_all |>
  group_by(window) |>
  mutate(
    resid_mean = mean(resid, na.rm = TRUE),
    resid_sd   = sd(resid, na.rm = TRUE),
    z_score    = (resid - resid_mean) / resid_sd
  ) |>
  ungroup()

results_all |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = z_score, color = window)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept =  2, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -2, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept =  0, linetype = "solid",  color = "grey70") +
  facet_wrap(~window, ncol = 1) +

    "60 days"  = "#d7191c",
    "252 days" = "#2c7bb6",
    "504 days" = "#1a9641"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Residual Z-score — Deviation from rolling equilibrium",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines at ±2σ — H2 signal",
    x = NULL, y = "Z-score", color = "Window"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Rolling OLS
text:
Interpretation
Rolling β : if the three windows consistently hover around zero over 2012–2024, the absence of a stable relationship is robust to window choice. The post-2025 explosion is likely a statistical artifact driven by gold’s strong upward trend against a range-bound yield.
Rolling R² : episodic peaks — notably around 2016 and during the COVID shock (2020) — suggest the relationship activates in specific macro regimes: periods of low inflation where the nominal yield closely tracks the real yield.
Z-score (H2) : in the absence of a stable cointegrating relationship, the Z-score does not constitute a mean-reversion signal in the strict sense. It measures the current deviation of gold relative to its historical average relationship with yields. A sustained Z-score above +2σ — as observed from 2024 onward — signals that gold is operating in a structurally different regime, likely driven by factors beyond Treasury yields (geopolitical risk, de-dollarization, central bank demand).

title: Gold & Treasury Yields — Rolling OLS
text:
Conclusion
The rolling OLS analysis delivers a clear and robust finding across all three window sizes: the nominal 10Y Treasury yield is not a structural explainer of gold prices.
The relationship is episodic. Periods of meaningful explanatory power — notably 2014–2016 and 2018–2022 — are visible in the 504-day R², reaching peaks above 0.75. However, these episodes are the exception rather than the rule over the full 2011–2026 sample.
This result is consistent with the theoretical limitation outlined in the introduction: the nominal yield embeds both the real rate and inflation expectations, two forces with opposing effects on gold. When inflation dominates — as it did post-2022 — the nominal yield loses its directional signal for gold, and the relationship breaks down or reverses.
The Z-score analysis reinforces this conclusion. From 2011 to approximately 2023, residuals fluctuate within the ±2σ band across all window sizes — consistent with a relationship operating near its historical average. From 2024 onward, all three windows show a sustained and extreme deviation above +2σ, peaking near +8σ on the 252-day window. This is not a mean-reversion signal — it is evidence of a structural regime change — driven by factors that lie outside the scope of this analysis and that the nominal yield alone cannot capture..
H1 (long-run cointegration between gold and nominal yield): not validated.
H2 (mean-reverting residual): partially validated — the signal holds in low-inflation regimes but breaks down when inflation expectations dominate the nominal yield signal.
These findings are discussed and synthesized in the general conclusion.
